scope: Selected PostgreSQL-backed job and queue ecosystem; not exhaustive. PostgreSQL paths only.

systems.name: Absurd
systems.tagline: Checkpointed workflows that replay persisted steps after interruption.
systems.summary: PostgreSQL durable workflows that replay task code and load persisted step results on retry.
systems.fit: Consider for long-running processes with durable sleep, external events and checkpoint replay. Requires stable workflow code/step identities and an external strategy for recurring schedules; compare contracts before comparing throughput.

snapshot.label: 0.5.1 · source snapshot
snapshot.note: Features reviewed against pinned default-branch source; release label is separately verified, not assumed to be the benchmark adapter version.

transaction.text: TypeScript bindToConnection runs spawn and other operations on a supplied database connection, allowing use inside an application transaction. The caller must own the transaction.

recovery.text: Workers claim a task for a bounded duration; checkpoint writes extend the claim. After expiration another worker can pick up the task; enough progress/headroom is required.

scheduling.text: Tasks can sleep or await cached named events. No built-in recurring scheduler: docs show an application scheduler or optional pg_cron plus spawn-time idempotency keys.

uniqueness.text: If a task with a matching queue-scoped idempotency key exists, spawn returns that task. Provider-side idempotency is separate.

extension.text: Core installs a SQL schema on PostgreSQL 14+. pg_cron is one optional recurring-scheduler approach, not a core prerequisite.

ui.text: Habitat is a separate Go application with an embedded SolidJS UI for tasks, runs, checkpoints and events; it connects directly to PostgreSQL.

concurrency.text: Workers pull tasks as capacity permits; SDK worker examples configure concurrency. This review did not verify a native fleet-wide concurrency or rate-limit primitive.

caveats.text: This is durable workflow/checkpoint execution, not the same contract as a plain job queue or visibility-timeout message queue.
A completed checkpoint prevents re-running that recorded step; it does not atomically commit arbitrary provider effects with the checkpoint.
Go SDK is described upstream as experimental bootstrap.

systems.effectBoundary: Retries replay completed checkpoint results. Task claims expire and can overlap briefly; a side effect before its checkpoint is persisted can still repeat, so external provider idempotency is required.
systems.commercial: Apache-2.0 project. No paid feature tier was identified in the reviewed primary docs.

sources.label: Checkpoints, claims, retries and external idempotency
Workflow code changes and checkpoint compatibility

systems.name: Awa
systems.tagline: Typed Rust and Python jobs with segmented storage and guarded attempts.
systems.summary: A Rust and Python job framework using PostgreSQL for enqueue, worker claims, recovery and operational state. The inspected development revision uses segmented queue storage and claim receipts.
systems.fit: Evaluate when Rust and Python workers need shared PostgreSQL jobs with transactional enqueue and operational controls. Test the deployed release, database settings and handler recovery behavior; the lab and old benchmark use different snapshots.

snapshot.label: 0.7.0-alpha.1 · development main
snapshot.note: The inspected main revision is newer than both the historical benchmark and released 0.6 packages. Development features are not claims about every release.

transaction.text: insert_with accepts the application’s PostgreSQL transaction executor. Business writes and enqueue can share one commit. The ordinary handler’s completion is separate; the ADR-042 caller-owned handler API is not implemented at this snapshot.

recovery.text: Heartbeat staleness and hard deadlines close abandoned attempts for retry/failure handling. Completion validates the open attempt identity; a rescued handler can still run late. Delivery is at least once.

scheduling.text: Future run_at, retry backoff and snooze use deferred storage. A maintenance leader drives periodic/cron schedules, including timezones; a live worker fleet performs scheduling and promotion.

uniqueness.text: Insert uniqueness is configurable by kind, queue, arguments and selected job states. It controls enqueue identity, not exactly-once handler execution or external effects.

extension.text: Awa installs SQL schemas and migrations on PostgreSQL, without a dedicated queue extension. Worker runtimes own maintenance; pg_cron is not required for its scheduler.

ui.text: The awa serve operational interface includes queues, jobs, cron and dead-letter management. Runtime and CLI versions must match the supported schema/upgrade contract.

concurrency.text: Per-queue worker permits and an optional weighted pool govern local runtime capacity. Do not interpret global_max_workers as an automatically fleet-wide limit. Multiple claimers share one runtime’s queue permits.

caveats.text: Queue-storage claim transactions use synchronous_commit=off. A claim acknowledged before its WAL is flushed may disappear after a database crash, leaving the job claimable again.
A stale-completion guard protects database state; it cannot stop an isolated old handler from calling an external service.
Segment rotation, storage trust checks and rolling upgrades are operational considerations; use the documentation for the deployed version.

systems.effectBoundary: External calls cannot join the PostgreSQL enqueue/completion atomicity boundary. The documented at-least-once contract requires duplicate-safe handlers or provider idempotency.
systems.commercial: This profile evaluates the MIT/Apache-2.0 open-source revision only.

systems.name: GoodJob
systems.tagline: A Rails ActiveJob backend with a dashboard and concurrency extensions.
systems.summary: A Postgres-backed ActiveJob backend for Rails with threads, scheduling, an integrated dashboard and concurrency extensions. Default job claims use advisory locks; current main also documents an experimental SKIP LOCKED mode.
systems.fit: Useful to evaluate when a Rails application wants an ActiveJob-native queue with operational UI and recurring jobs. Compare its default advisory mode separately from the newer experimental SKIP LOCKED mode when planning connection pooling or upgrades.

snapshot.label: 4.22.1 · main
snapshot.note: Feature claims below describe this pinned source snapshot; the version constant is not evidence that all changes at HEAD shipped in that release.

transaction.text: Enqueue persists a GoodJob::Job via ActiveRecord save!. The adapter’s enqueue_after_transaction_commit setting defaults false. Sharing the application’s database connection and keeping enqueue inside its transaction can make the insert atomic; using a separate connection/database or deferred enqueue changes that boundary. This is a source-derived conditional claim.

recovery.text: Docs say interrupted jobs are automatically retried, including SIGKILL/power failure. Ordinary exceptions instead rely on ActiveJob retry_on by default. GoodJob.retry_on_unhandled_error=true enables immediate infinite retries and docs warn of high load.

scheduling.text: ActiveJob delayed jobs and built-in cron are documented. Cron is opt-in (enable_cron); unique indexes suppress duplicate enqueue of a given fire interval, requiring preserved cron job records.

uniqueness.text: GoodJob extensions offer enqueue/perform/total limits and throttles scoped by labels, plus cron-fire uniqueness. Docs warn about some state/race nuances and describe optimistic retry for perform limits. Do not equate those controls with exactly-once external effects.

extension.text: README explicitly says the advisory-lock key derivation does not require PostgreSQL extensions. Compatibility section lists Postgres10+, Rails6.1+ and Ruby3.0+ for this snapshot.

ui.text: Core README includes a mounted dashboard with job browsing, retries, cron and related operational views.

concurrency.text: Default claims use session-level advisory locks. Current main documents :skiplocked, which writes lock state to the jobs table, and :hybrid for mixed rolling deployments. This snapshot evidence does not establish that those main changes are in the latest release.

caveats.text: Unhandled task errors are not retried by default; configure ActiveJob retry_on or explicitly choose GoodJob’s unhandled-error behavior. Interrupted processes are handled separately.
Default advisory locks and LISTEN need persistent connections. Experimental skiplocked mode has additional required settings for transaction pooling.
Concurrency limits and cron deduplication have different semantics from an external-provider idempotency key.
Features are sourced from pinned main after the v4.22.1 release; do not assume every main change shipped in 4.22.1.

systems.effectBoundary: Because interrupted executions are retried, an external effect performed before interruption may repeat. This is an inference from documented recovery; the README’s run-once wording is not treated as a guarantee of exactly-once external effects.
systems.commercial: Only the MIT upstream core was evaluated. No separate commercial feature tier is asserted.

systems.name: Graphile Worker
systems.tagline: Node.js task executors, SQL enqueue and serial named queues.
systems.summary: Node.js task executors with SQL enqueue, serial named queues and retryable PostgreSQL jobs.
systems.fit: A natural candidate when Node task executors and SQL-triggered enqueue fit the application. Evaluate the OSS crash-unlock delay and migration workflow against operational recovery targets.

snapshot.label: v0.18.0 · source snapshot
snapshot.note: Features reviewed against pinned default-branch source; release label is separately verified, not assumed to be the benchmark adapter version.

transaction.text: Call graphile_worker.add_job from the application transaction or a trigger; work is visible after commit.

recovery.text: Abruptly terminated OSS workers leave jobs locked for at least four hours; periodic sweeps unlock them. Faster tracked-worker recovery is a proprietary Worker Pro feature.

scheduling.text: run_at defers a job; the built-in UTC crontab can backfill missed schedules when configured. Recurring scheduling and eventual execution are distinct.

uniqueness.text: job_key can replace/debounce unlocked jobs; default modes enqueue a new job if the prior matching job is locked. Completed jobs are deleted, so this is not permanent deduplication.

extension.text: Requirements say pgcrypto is no longer used since v0.13. PostgreSQL 12+ and Node 22.18+ are documented current requirements.

ui.text: A bundled first-party operational dashboard was not verified in this review; this does not mean third-party UIs do not exist.

concurrency.text: Named queue jobs execute one at a time. Claim SQL uses FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. This is distinct from global provider rate limiting.

caveats.text: Do not describe Worker Pro recovery as an OSS default; abrupt-death recovery is materially different.
unsafe_dedupe may suppress triggering work; job keys are not a provider-side exactly-once guarantee.

systems.effectBoundary: The introduction specifies at-least-once execution; failures retry. External side effects still need an idempotent design.
systems.commercial: MIT core. Worker Pro is proprietary/source-available and adds live migration plus faster crashed-worker recovery. No price comparison is made.

systems.name: Oban
systems.tagline: An Ecto and OTP job framework with queues, retries and telemetry.
systems.summary: An Ecto and OTP job framework with queues, retries and telemetry.
systems.fit: An Elixir/OTP and Ecto-oriented job framework with retained job history, isolated queues, scheduled work and telemetry. Choose queue limits and engine deliberately when distributing across nodes.

snapshot.label: 2.24.2 · source snapshot
snapshot.note: Release version comes from official Hex package metadata, not the older GitHub latest-release record. Scope is the Elixir OSS package; the separate Python implementation is not profiled here.

transaction.text: Oban.insert integrates with Ecto.Multi so enqueue and other database changes share one commit.

recovery.text: At-least-once execution with retries/backoff and a configured attempt limit. Abandoned executing jobs require a configured rescue service such as OSS Oban.Lifeline; its age-based policy can rescue genuinely running jobs too. Pro Lifeline offers more accurate rescue.

scheduling.text: Future scheduling and cron-like periodic jobs are part of OSS. Pro Dynamic plugins add runtime schedule and queue management.

uniqueness.text: OSS insertion-time uniqueness uses transactional locks and queries and can race in some circumstances; it does not serialize execution. Pro Smart Engine uses unique constraints for stronger guarantees.

extension.text: The PostgreSQL engine is an Elixir/Ecto library and schema migrations; documented prerequisites include PostgreSQL 14+, Elixir 1.15+ and Erlang 24+, not a custom queue extension.

ui.text: Oban Web is now free and open source under Apache-2.0, with an embedded Phoenix LiveView dashboard and an optional standalone image. It can expose paid Pro controls when Pro is installed. Older commercially licensed Web releases are not the current distribution.

concurrency.text: The PostgreSQL Basic engine claims using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED with a local queue limit. Pro Smart Engine supplies global concurrency, global rate limits and partitioning.

caveats.text: Insert uniqueness is not concurrent-execution exclusion.
Global rate/concurrency controls belong to Pro; the current official dashboard itself is open source.
This profile covers the Elixir PostgreSQL package although the ecosystem also has a Python implementation and alternate SQL engines.

systems.effectBoundary: Application-level inference: recovery or repeated consumption may repeat external operations. Database transaction or acknowledgement guarantees do not, by themselves, atomically include another provider’s effects.
systems.commercial: Oban Pro provides Smart Engine, workflows, batches and dynamic plugins; do not attribute these to the OSS Basic engine.

systems.name: pg-boss
systems.tagline: Node.js job queues with explicit queue policies and transaction adapters.
systems.summary: PostgreSQL job queues with configurable duplicate policies, retries, scheduling and transaction adapters.
systems.fit: Consider when a Node application needs database transaction adapters plus queue policy controls. Choose heartbeat, expiration and worker transaction settings explicitly for your workload.

snapshot.label: 12.38.0 · source snapshot
snapshot.note: Features reviewed against pinned default-branch source; release label is separately verified, not assumed to be the benchmark adapter version.

transaction.text: send, insert, fetch and complete accept a db transaction adapter. transactional workers can commit same-database handler SQL with completion. External API calls are outside that transaction.

recovery.text: Heartbeat detection is disabled by default; expiration defaults to 15 minutes. Both route to retry/failure policy. Late settlement is guarded by the claimed retryCount.

scheduling.text: Schedules need a running instance; evaluation has minute-level filing precision. Catch-up is skip by default, with a once policy for missed occurrences.

uniqueness.text: standard, short, singleton, stately, exclusive and key_strict_fifo policies have different queued/active constraints and can use singletonKey. These are not permanent external-effect deduplication.

extension.text: Stock PostgreSQL is the primary backend; installation creates pg-boss schema objects. Current package requires Node >=22.12; overview lists PostgreSQL >=13.

ui.text: @pg-boss/dashboard is documented for queues, jobs and schedules; this is a separate package, not a claim about older benchmark versions.

concurrency.text: localConcurrency is per process. Group concurrency options and queue policies have separate scopes; do not treat a per-process number as a fleet-wide limit.

caveats.text: A partitioned or event-loop-stalled old handler may still execute after rescue, despite guarded completion.
Transactional workers hold a connection and transaction for handler duration; long jobs can delay vacuum.

systems.effectBoundary: Current introduction explicitly says worker crashes or expiration can cause a handler to run again; handlers must tolerate repeats.
systems.commercial: MIT project. The reviewed first-party docs do not identify a paid feature tier for these listed capabilities.

systems.name: PGMQ
systems.tagline: SQL messages with a visibility timeout and application-owned consumers.
systems.summary: SQL messages with a visibility timeout and application-owned consumers.
systems.fit: A SQL message primitive for applications that want control over polling, visibility renewal, acknowledgement and archival. It is a smaller delivery contract than a framework that owns handlers, attempt budgets and job lifecycles.

snapshot.label: v1.13.1 · source snapshot
snapshot.note: Features reviewed at this pinned revision. Release names are not the benchmark adapter version.

transaction.text: pgmq.send is a SQL INSERT function, so producers can call it inside the same PostgreSQL transaction as application writes. This is a database API, not a separate broker.

recovery.text: read hides a message for a visibility timeout; if it is not deleted or archived, it becomes available again. The upstream exactly-once wording is limited to that timeout and is not an external-side-effect guarantee.

scheduling.text: send and send_batch accept relative delays or timestamps. No recurring/cron job scheduler was verified in the reviewed core API.

uniqueness.text: No insertion deduplication guarantee was verified for the reviewed send API. FIFO group ordering is a different feature from deduplication.

extension.text: The upstream supports both packaged pgmq extension installation and SQL-only installation of its objects. The benchmark repository uses the extension distribution. Current README states PostgreSQL 14–18.

ui.text: No official standalone operations dashboard was verified in the reviewed upstream core sources.

concurrency.text: SQL reads lock selected rows with SKIP LOCKED and update visibility/read count. Application consumers choose their worker counts; FIFO group APIs provide a separate ordering mode.

caveats.text: Applications must set or extend visibility appropriately and explicitly delete/archive after success.
There is no verified core automatic exponential backoff/max-attempt job policy; read_ct is available for application policy.
External operations can repeat after visibility expiry.

systems.effectBoundary: Application-level inference: recovery or repeated consumption may repeat external operations. Database transaction or acknowledgement guarantees do not, by themselves, atomically include another provider’s effects.
systems.commercial: The reviewed upstream core has the PostgreSQL license; no paid feature split was identified there. Hosted products and third-party clients are outside this profile.

systems.name: PgQ
systems.tagline: The maintained original PgQ event engine, with tick-based batches.
systems.summary: The maintained original PgQ event engine, with tick-based batches.
systems.fit: Relevant when batch event-stream consumption and existing PgQ tooling are the required contract. Deployment needs the extension and a ticker/maintenance process; verify managed-provider support.

snapshot.label: v3.5.2 · source snapshot
snapshot.note: Maintained engine is pgq/pgq. pgq/skytools redirects to archived skytools-legacy, and markokr/skytools labels itself legacy. Do not confuse the engine with NikolayS/PgQue or que-rb/que.

transaction.text: SQL insert_event inserts into the queue within the caller transaction; snapshot/tick batches track committed event windows.

recovery.text: An active unfinished batch is returned again by next_batch. event_retry schedules an event at an absolute or relative time. Consumers own processing and when to finish a batch.

scheduling.text: event_retry supports future redelivery times. No current first-class per-job cron API was verified in the engine sources reviewed.

uniqueness.text: No general unique-job producer API was verified. event_retry handles repeated retry insertion idempotently, which is a narrower operation.

extension.text: PgQ is a PostgreSQL extension with C low-level functions. pgqd is a separate maintenance/ticker daemon. Current engine README lists PostgreSQL 10–19.

ui.text: No current official operations UI was verified in the reviewed engine and daemon documentation.

concurrency.text: Work is grouped by tick windows and registered-consumer position rather than a per-job running row. Multiple-consumer/cooperative tooling belongs to the surrounding PgQ ecosystem; its full topology was not audited.

caveats.text: It is an event queue engine, not a drop-in handler framework with a verified current unique-jobs/cron/UI surface.
External effects remain outside PostgreSQL transaction/ack boundaries.

systems.effectBoundary: Application-level inference: recovery or repeated consumption may repeat external operations. Database transaction or acknowledgement guarantees do not, by themselves, atomically include another provider’s effects.
systems.commercial: Maintained PgQ engine is ISC licensed. No commercial feature split was identified in the reviewed core.

systems.name: PgQue
systems.tagline: A shared event log with consumer cursors and batch acknowledgements.
systems.summary: A shared event log with consumer cursors and batch acknowledgements.
systems.fit: A shared event-log and fan-out design when independently advancing consumer groups and batch acknowledgement match the workload. Ticking and maintenance are explicit operating responsibilities.

snapshot.label: v0.2.2 · source snapshot
snapshot.note: Repository .gitmodules points to https://github.com/NikolayS/pgque.git, whose canonical GitHub spelling is NikolayS/PgQue. Distinct from pgq/pgq. Current main can contain changes beyond v0.2.2.

transaction.text: send can join business writes. receive, local database writes and batch ack can commit together; send, ticker and receive must not be collapsed into one transaction because of snapshot visibility.

recovery.text: Default consumption is at least once. nack schedules a per-event retry and routes exhausted events to a dead-letter table; the application still acknowledges the whole received batch.

scheduling.text: Recurring production can use pg_cron. Delayed send_at is an explicitly loaded experimental add-on, not the default stable API.

uniqueness.text: No general insert-time unique-job API was verified in the reviewed default interface. Idempotent retry/DLQ operations are not producer deduplication.

extension.text: Default installation is SQL/PLpgSQL on PostgreSQL 14+ without a C extension. A ticker and maintenance must be driven by pg_cron, pg_timetable or an external process; optional pg_tle packaging has different prerequisites.

ui.text: The repository web directory is its marketing/documentation site, not evidence of an operations dashboard.

concurrency.text: Independent registered consumers each keep a cursor over the shared log. Cooperative subconsumers are experimental; allocation serializes on a subscription row. This is not the default per-job competing-consumer contract.

caveats.text: Upstream calls the product/API early-stage; mature PgQ ancestry is not the same as mature new interfaces.
receive returns a whole batch or errors; max_return is a safety ceiling, not pagination.
Cooperative consumers and delayed delivery have explicit experimental status.
Batch-ID APIs do not enforce per-consumer ownership; roles must be designed accordingly.

systems.effectBoundary: Application-level inference: recovery or repeated consumption may repeat external operations. Database transaction or acknowledgement guarantees do not, by themselves, atomically include another provider’s effects.
systems.commercial: The reviewed project uses Apache-2.0 with ISC-derived PgQ code acknowledged in NOTICE; no paid edition was verified.

sources.label: Replace autoattached refs with early-stage status source
Use exact whole-batch receive ceiling source

systems.name: PotatoQ
systems.tagline: An alpha Python worker with Celery-shaped APIs and a Postgres transport.
systems.summary: A Python task queue with Postgres, SQLite, Redis/Valkey and RabbitMQ transports. The Postgres transport uses short SKIP LOCKED claims and late acknowledgement, with an optional application-owned transaction for enqueue.
systems.fit: Useful to evaluate when a Python application wants Celery-shaped task APIs, Django Tasks integration and a Postgres transport without a separate broker. The alpha status and transport-specific behavior make pinning and application-level failure tests particularly important.

snapshot.label: 26.1a8 (alpha)
snapshot.note: Feature claims below describe this pinned source snapshot; the version constant is not evidence that all changes at HEAD shipped in that release.

transaction.text: For the Postgres transport, enqueue(messages, connection=...) uses the caller’s DB-API connection. Django/SQLAlchemy integrations do this for a matching database. Otherwise enqueue is deferred until commit, which retains a commit-to-publish failure window.

recovery.text: Task removal follows completion. Child-process death requeues work; a missing node is recovered after worker_dead_after (default60 s). After task_max_deliveries (default5) crashed deliveries it is dead-lettered. Task exceptions are not retried by default; retry/autoretry is opt-in.

scheduling.text: ETAs/retries remain in the broker; workers promote due Postgres tasks. Every worker may schedule recurring tasks; Postgres deduplicates each (entry, fire_time) by a unique row in the same transaction as enqueue. This is schedule-fire deduplication, not generic task uniqueness.

uniqueness.text: Arbitrary unique-task/deduplication keys and per-key concurrency limits are explicitly wishlist items. Periodic-fire deduplication is a separate implemented mechanism.

extension.text: The Postgres broker creates regular tables and indexes itself; psycopg3 is the transport dependency. Docs require Postgres13+; Django’s minimum may be higher.

ui.text: The package includes a dashboard for workers, queues, periodic tasks, task details and dead-letter replay. It works with every broker; this is documented functionality, not measured in this repository.

concurrency.text: A MATERIALIZED CTE selects one job with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; the UPDATE gives the delivery a random token. Completion’s fenced DELETE matches id, running state and token before writing results/follow-ups. No transaction spans task execution.

caveats.text: Explicitly alpha; API and defaults may change.
Post-commit callbacks for a different broker do not have the atomicity of same-connection Postgres enqueue.
Task rate_limit is accepted with a warning but not enforced; generic unique-task keys and per-key concurrency limits are wishlist items.
This profile covers the Postgres transport; other broker transports have different transaction and recovery behavior.

systems.effectBoundary: At-least-once delivery and claim fencing do not make an external API side effect atomic with Postgres completion. The application/provider must make repeated external operations safe. This is an inference from the documented at-least-once contract and separate result/ack transaction, not a new provider guarantee.
systems.commercial: Only the MIT upstream core was evaluated. No separate commercial feature tier is asserted.

sources.label: Canonical project link from official docs

systems.name: Procrastinate
systems.tagline: Python sync/async tasks with application locks and configurable recovery.
systems.summary: Sync and async Python tasks with PostgreSQL scheduling, application locks and optional Django integration.
systems.fit: A Python-focused option when sync/async code or Django integration is useful. Useful when application-level serialization keys are needed, with recovery tasks and retry policies configured deliberately.

snapshot.label: 3.10.0 · source snapshot
snapshot.note: Features reviewed against pinned default-branch source; release label is separately verified, not assumed to be the benchmark adapter version.

transaction.text: configure(connection=...) defers on an application-owned transaction with supported psycopg or SQLAlchemy connectors; caller commits. This is current default-branch behavior, not an assertion about older adapter pins.

recovery.text: Heartbeats identify stalled workers, but crashed jobs may remain doing forever unless an operator or configured periodic task retries them.

scheduling.text: schedule_at / schedule_in defer jobs; App.periodic implements cron with distributed once-per-period enqueue. A worker must be running for periodic enqueue.

uniqueness.text: queueing_lock rejects another pending todo job via AlreadyEnqueued; it permits multiple doing jobs. Combine with an execution lock if serialized execution is also needed.

extension.text: The installed schema consists of SQL tables/functions; docs specify Python 3.10+ and PostgreSQL 13+, with no extra queue service.

ui.text: Procrastinate exposes job/event/periodic models in Django admin; models are read-only by default. This is an optional Django integration, not a standalone bundled dashboard.

concurrency.text: Worker concurrency is configurable. lock strings serialize jobs sharing a key; priority then creation time determine order among waiting jobs. Claims use FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.

caveats.text: Retrying after abrupt worker death is not automatic unless you configure stalled-job recovery.
Queueing lock prevents a second todo entry, not overlapping doing entries or duplicate external side effects.

systems.effectBoundary: Jobs can repeat when retried; retries are opt-in and default to no retry. Stalled-worker recovery also requires explicit configuration, so do not present unconditional automatic eventual delivery.
systems.commercial: MIT project; no paid feature tier was identified in the reviewed primary docs.

systems.name: Que
systems.tagline: A focused Ruby queue built around advisory locks and transaction control.
systems.summary: A Ruby/Postgres job queue built around session advisory locks, multithreaded workers and database transactions. Native Que jobs can put application writes and job destruction inside the same transaction.
systems.fit: A focused choice to evaluate for Ruby applications using ActiveRecord or Sequel that want transaction control without a separate broker. Native Que jobs expose stronger database integration than the generic ActiveJob adapter.

snapshot.label: 2.4.1 · source
snapshot.note: Pinned master source reports version 2.4.1. GitHub’s latest non-prerelease release endpoint reported v2.4.0 (2024-08-20), so its date is not presented as the release date of this 2.4.1 source snapshot.

transaction.text: Enqueue can piggyback on ActiveRecord/Sequel connections and commit or roll back with application data. Native Que jobs may destroy/finish themselves in the same application transaction. Docs warn the ActiveJob adapter loses the ability to finish a job inside the same transaction as other operations.

recovery.text: Advisory locks disappear when a worker’s connection dies, making unfinished jobs available. Error retries use an increasing interval and maximum_retry_count; docs describe a default15 retries. Crash recovery can repeat a partially completed handler.

scheduling.text: Native jobs support future run_at and priority. The README lists que-scheduler as a separate cron-style project, under related projects described as tested for Que1.x; current2.x compatibility is unverified.

uniqueness.text: No general native uniqueness feature was verified. README links que-unique and que-locks as companion projects tested with Que1.x; this is not evidence of bundled2.x deduplication.

extension.text: The documented setup migrates Que’s schema in PostgreSQL; no separate Postgres extension is specified. README’s server minimum is PostgreSQL9.5+.

ui.text: README lists que-web and que-view, not a bundled UI, and labels those related projects as Que1.x-compatible. Compatibility with this2.x snapshot was not checked.

concurrency.text: Workers coordinate with PostgreSQL advisory locks; the worker process is multithreaded. Locking does not itself require updating the job row.

caveats.text: The core docs explicitly allow repeated execution after a crash; external side effects still require duplicate-safe design.
Session advisory locking needs a direct/session connection; a separate connection-url can bypass transaction-pooled app connections.
Long transactions can prevent vacuum cleanup and degrade the high-churn job table.
The related scheduler/UI/uniqueness projects are listed as Que 1.x-compatible; compatibility with this2.x snapshot was not verified.

systems.effectBoundary: Writing Reliable Jobs documents the crash window between an external operation and job destruction, including possible repeated email/payment effects.
systems.commercial: Only the MIT upstream core was evaluated. No separate commercial feature tier is asserted.

systems.name: River
systems.tagline: A PostgreSQL job framework with a shared format across language clients.
systems.summary: A PostgreSQL job framework with a shared format across language clients.
systems.fit: Useful when a PostgreSQL job lifecycle and transactional application integration are central; current clients share a cross-language job format. The repository benchmark measures the Go adapter, not every language implementation.

snapshot.label: Go v0.49.0 · source snapshot
snapshot.note: Repository latest-release endpoint currently returns a Ruby package release; Go module latest was verified separately. Current docs cover multiple languages and SQLite as well as PostgreSQL. Benchmark adapter Go version is separate.

transaction.text: InsertTx can commit a job atomically with application changes in the same PostgreSQL transaction. Go also supports JobCompleteTx for completion plus local writes; this does not cover external side effects.

recovery.text: Ordinary workers execute at least once; failed completion persistence or a process crash may cause another execution. Retry policy is configurable with a finite attempt budget.

scheduling.text: Delayed jobs and periodic/cron insertion are available. OSS periodic schedules are held in leader memory and reset across restarts/elections; durable periodic schedules are Pro.

uniqueness.text: Unique jobs use a partial unique index and selected argument, kind, period, queue and state dimensions. Uniqueness controls insertion, not exactly-once execution.

extension.text: The reviewed PostgreSQL runtime uses schema migrations and standard SQL tables/functions, rather than a dedicated queue extension.

ui.text: River UI has an official open-source base variant; the Pro UI requires River Pro.

concurrency.text: PostgreSQL claims use FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; OSS clients set per-queue worker counts. Cluster-wide concurrency controls are a Pro feature.

caveats.text: At-least-once execution means an external operation still needs duplicate-safe handling.
Go timeouts rely on context cooperation.
Distinguish OSS worker limits and in-memory periodic schedules from their Pro counterparts.

Language implementations share a schema/protocol but do not have identical APIs or verified full mixed-language runtime coverage. Ruby currently lacks transactional job completion; its docs recommend thread-based production workers rather than Ractors. Java exists as a separate prerelease and is outside this profile.

systems.effectBoundary: Application-level inference: recovery or repeated consumption may repeat external operations. Database transaction or acknowledgement guarantees do not, by themselves, atomically include another provider’s effects.
systems.commercial: River Pro adds paid extensions. The reviewed Go documentation distributes Pro as a private module; the Ruby docs describe a separate private riverqueue-pro gem. Feature/API parity across SDKs was not established.

sources.label: Avoid implying only Go has a commercial implementation

systems.name: Solid Queue
systems.tagline: Rails job infrastructure with SQL dispatch and explicit failure records.
systems.summary: A database-backed Rails ActiveJob backend supporting PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite. It combines short SKIP LOCKED polling with separate ready/scheduled/failed execution records and process supervision.
systems.fit: Useful to evaluate for Rails applications seeking a framework-integrated database queue, especially when portability beyond Postgres matters. Its separate queue-database default and explicit failed-job handling need to fit the application’s transaction and recovery expectations.

snapshot.label: 1.7.0 · main
snapshot.note: Feature claims below describe this pinned source snapshot; the version constant is not evidence that all changes at HEAD shipped in that release.

transaction.text: Docs describe transactional enqueue when jobs share the application database/connection and transaction, but default configuration uses a different database. Rails enqueue_after_transaction_commit defers enqueue after commit and does not provide the same atomic handoff.

recovery.text: Expired process heartbeats and abnormal process exits mark claimed jobs failed with ProcessPrunedError/ProcessExitError. Docs explicitly say these are not automatically retried; ActiveJob retry_on cannot catch errors recorded after the process has died. FailedExecution#retry or external automation can re-enqueue them.

scheduling.text: Delayed work is dispatched when due; recurring tasks use a scheduler and recurring.yml, with Fugit schedule parsing.

uniqueness.text: limits_concurrency uses key/group semaphores. Default conflicts block; on_conflict:discard can suppress conflicting enqueues. Duration is a release failsafe and does not establish strict execution order or universal exactly-once effects.

extension.text: The documented Postgres path uses regular tables and SKIP LOCKED, with no additional Postgres extension specified. Rails/ActiveJob dependencies and schema migration remain required.

ui.text: README points to Mission Control—Jobs as a dashboard rather than describing a bundled Solid Queue UI. Its installation/version was not separately audited here.

concurrency.text: PostgreSQL9.5+ supports the SKIP LOCKED path used to avoid waiting behind other workers. Workers, dispatchers and scheduler have different roles; process heartbeats, not handler deadlines, track liveness.

caveats.text: By default the queue uses a separate database, so application-write/queue-insert atomicity must not be assumed.
Abrupt worker death marks in-flight work failed; automatic recovery retry is deliberately not provided. ActiveJob retry_on does not catch process-prune errors recorded by a surviving process.
Concurrency controls are time-bounded semaphores; expiry is not a hard guarantee that an old process stopped.
Features describe pinned main after release1.7.0; no assumption every current-main change shipped in1.7.0.

systems.effectBoundary: Application SQL and a queue row can share a transaction only under the documented conditions; external network effects cannot be included in that database atomicity. Retrying a failed or interrupted operation must account for already-performed effects. This is an application-level inference, not a new delivery guarantee.
systems.commercial: Only the MIT upstream core was evaluated. No separate commercial feature tier is asserted.
